entries.title: Popular Does Not Mean Right for Your Group

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: In our fictional example, a busy evening event gets lots of excited reviews. Your friend needs somewhere quiet to talk. Which question helps you choose? First: How many people liked it?

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Second: Will it be quiet enough for our conversation? Popularity tells you other people enjoyed something. It doesn't tell you whether the same place fits your purpose. Start with what your group actually needs.

entries.prompt: Which question checks your group's needs: the first or the second?
entries.answer: The second. Ask whether it will be quiet enough to talk.

entries.title: Crunchy and Salty Describe Different Things

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: This cracker is crunchy and salty. Are those two words telling you the same thing?

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: No. Crunchy describes the texture: how it feels when you bite. Salty describes the taste. You can use both to help someone imagine the snack.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: So a crunchy snack doesn't have to be salty. It could be crunchy and sweet, like some biscuits.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Exactly. Describe the food you actually tried. One word for texture and one for taste is a useful start.

entries.prompt: Which word describes taste: crunchy or salty?
entries.answer: Salty describes taste. Crunchy describes texture.

entries.title: An Honest Review Can Still Miss Your Needs
entries.hook: The review can be true and still not help.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Riley reads an excited review of a fictional evening event. The writer loved the loud music and busy crowd. Riley wants a quiet place to catch up with a friend. She doesn't need to call the review dishonest.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Instead, she says: That sounds fun for them, but it may not suit our plans. The writer describes a real preference inside this invented story. Riley has a different purpose. She looks for details about noise and seating, not just another enthusiastic opinion.

entries.prompt: Must the review be false because Riley wants a different kind of evening?
entries.answer: No. Different people can enjoy different things. Check the details that matter to your plans.

entries.title: Too Chewy for Me Is a Personal Preference

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: I brought these chewy sweets for us to try. You look unsure. Do you think they're terrible?

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Not terrible. They're a little too chewy for me. I prefer something softer. For me shows that I'm describing my own preference, not making a rule for everyone.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: I like chewy sweets, but now I know what you prefer. Would you rather try this soft cake?

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Yes, thanks. I can appreciate you sharing food without pretending to enjoy every texture. A clear, friendly answer helps you offer something different.

entries.prompt: Does too chewy for me mean nobody should like the sweet?
entries.answer: No. It describes one person's preference. Someone else may enjoy the same texture.
